title: The naive framing: "a full day of reading"
text: People assume researching a market means burying a full day in articles. It doesn't point Claude at the sources and that day compresses to about an hour. So, what does that hour actually get you?

title: You already do this
text: You might not call yourself a researcher, but if you've ever spent an afternoon reading articles to understand a market before entering it or pulled together everything on a competitor before a pitch, that's the work. You've done it. It just never made it onto the calendar. Here's what it usually looks like. An

title: The afternoon that vanishes
text: Afternoon vanishing into open tabs and printouts trying to hold a stack of sources in your head at once. Useful work, but slow and easy to keep postponing. Point research support at the same pile

title: A day into an hour
text: And the shape changes. Give it a topic and a set of sources and you get in about an hour what used to take a day of reading and note-taking. The bottleneck was never your intelligence. It was your time. Give Claude a topic and a stack of

title: Sources in, meaning out
text: Sources, articles, reports, documents and it pulls out the common themes, the places they conflict and the takeaways that matter. Your sources flow in, structured understanding comes out. The

title: What they mean together
text: Difference that matters, it doesn't tell you what each source says one by one. It tells you what they mean together. A pile of separate accounts becomes one picture, the through line no single article stated on its own. That's the line between summary and

title: Summary versus synthesis
text: Synthesis. A summary just shrinks each source. Synthesis reads across them and it's the version you can actually make a decision on. Pointed at your market, the same engine

title: Four scouting jobs
text: Does four jobs: competitor intelligence, a structured market review, gap analysis what's covered and what isn't, and citation tracking so every claim keeps its source. Competitor intelligence

title: Reading the rivals
text: First. Claude reads how rivals position themselves, what they're building, how they talk to customers and where the gaps sit. It works from public information and gets sharper if you've saved their materials to your folders. What comes back is a map, not a list,

title: The anchor: the empty quadrant
text: Where each competitor sits on price and focus, who's crowded together and the corner nobody's standing in. That empty quadrant is often the whole point of the exercise. Hold on to it. Every finding

title: Every claim, sourced
text: Stays attached to where it came from. Ask for proper attribution and Claude tracks the sources and formats the citations, and it'll hook into a reference manager if you already run one. Gap analysis runs the same move on your

title: Find the hole
text: Own coverage. After reading across a topic, Claude shows what's been handled well and what's thin in the market or in your own research. You see the whole before it costs you. Most of this rides on how you ask. For a

title: Ask it precisely
text: Competitor deep dive, you type something like this. Everything public on their positioning, pricing model, audience, recent launches, and customer sentiment, then the strengths and weaknesses. Specific in, specific out. Or point it a

title: Your own shelf
text: Batch you've already collected. Drop a folder of articles on a topic into Claude work and ask for the trends they agree on, the places they disagree, and what it means for you specifically. Synthesis on your own shelf. Say you're weighing a new market. Ask

title: One structured briefing
text: Claude to research it. How big, who's already there, what customers actually need, where the openings are, and it returns a structured briefing. Context, players, pain points, opportunity gaps, and the things to watch. But the output is only as sharp as the

title: Purpose shapes the output
text: Purpose you name. Research AI trends gives you a bland overview. Research AI trends so I can decide whether to add AI services to my practice gives you focused usable intelligence. The purpose shapes the answer.

title: The anchor returns: the edge of a decision
text: This is the moment research is really for. Standing at the edge of a decision you can't take back, maybe eyeing the empty quadrant you spotted in the competitor map. Better to have scouted the ground first than to find out after you've stepped. For a straight choice,

title: Options, side by side
text: Say a free trial model versus a freemium one, ask for the advantages and drawbacks of each for your kind of product with real examples. Claude lays them side by side on the evidence, so you're deciding on a comparison instead of a gut feeling. Here's the discipline. Treat what comes

title: Leads, not verdicts
text: Back as leads, not verdicts. A finding that lines up with what you expected doesn't confirm it's true. The scout can be confidently wrong. And a finding that surprises you doesn't confirm it's false either. It might be exactly the gap you needed to see. Either way, verify the load-bearing claims, check the sources, and keep the judgment yours. And when sources disagree, don't smooth

title: Keep the disagreements
text: It over. Ask Claude to flag the contradictions and leave them standing. Experts disagreeing isn't a mess to clean up. It's a map of where the real uncertainty lies, and that's information you want. Which leaves one habit worth

title: Head down, delivering
text: Building. Picture the operator with their head down in delivery, shipping the work, never once looking up at the market moving around them. Now, the one who spends an hour a month

title: Head up, deciding
text: Scouting, who knows their market cold, same desk, window open, same effort, better decisions. That's the whole return on the habit. Set the time aside and let Claude do the scouting. Research support turns your sources into

title: Carry-out
text: Synthesis, not summary, but every finding it hands back is a lead to verify, never a verdict to trust outright. Your turn. Paste this into Claude. I'm

title: Your turn
text: Considering entering a market. Act as my scout. Size it, name who's already there, map the competitors in the gaps, tell me the three things customers actually need, and flag every claim you're unsure about so I know what to verify. It turns this into a scouting run on your real market, and notice it marks its own soft spots, which is exactly where your judgment comes in. Claude scouting the research plugin.
